tts: The world's most wanted watch was invented by a German in London. And it's owned not by a billionaire, but by a charitable foundation.
In nineteen-oh-five, Hans Wilsdorf started a London firm selling watches with Swiss movements. In nineteen-oh-eight, he made up the word Rolex: short, and it sounds the same in any language.
After World War One, British import duties rose, and in nineteen nineteen the company moved to Geneva.
In nineteen twenty-six, Rolex made the first waterproof wristwatch, the Oyster. Swimmer Mercedes Gleitze wore one for ten hours in the freezing English Channel, and it kept ticking.
Then came the legends: self-winding, the top of Everest, and in nineteen sixty, a Rolex rode a submersible to the bottom of the Mariana Trench and came back in one piece.
After his wife died, Wilsdorf created a foundation and left it the company. Rolex has no shareholders and publishes no accounts.
It makes more than a million watches a year, yet popular models are almost never in stores: there are waitlists.
Analysts estimate Rolex brings in about eleven billion Swiss francs a year. Not bad for a word made up in London.
